effect_estimate.comment: Cross-sectional mixed-effects logistic regressions were estimated separately by survey year; Table 6 prints the WSP mOR 95% CI as 5.93–98.48 (rounded to 5.93–98.5 in the Abstract and p. 10 text) and WSP uOR as 6.7 (2.71–16.57) versus 6.70 (2.70–16.57) in p. 8 text. Table 1 prints 2016 median water consumption as 63.5 lpcd whereas p. 5 text prints 65.3 lpcd.
effect_estimate.value: Between 2016 (n = 1,281) and 2017 (n = 1,360), piped network water as main household source declined from 22.0% to 15.3% (p < 0.001) while unregulated private water trucking rose from 77.0% to 82.5% (p < 0.001). Households spent a mean of 20.5% (SD 13.1%) of income on water in 2016 and 21.9% (SD 15.4%) in 2017 (p < 0.001), with share of income spent on water positively associated with childhood diarrhea in 2016 (mOR = 1.03, 95% CI: 1.02–1.04, p < 0.05), and 75.2% (2016) and 74.4% (2017) could not find or afford hygiene items (>95% citing affordability for most items). Community Water Safety Plan (WSP) risk-management programming expanded from 35.4% to 41.3% of households (p = 0.002), while household water with free chlorine residual (FCR) > 0.1 mg/L rose from 4.1% to 27.9% (p < 0.001). In 2017 regressions, WSP inclusion was strongly associated with FCR > 0.1 mg/L (uOR = 6.7, 95% CI: 2.71–16.57; aOR = 9.75, 95% CI: 6.85–14.05, p < 0.05; mixed-effect mOR = 24.16, 95% CI: 5.93–98.48 [reported as 5.93–98.5 in text], p < 0.05), whereas piped network vs. trucked main source had lower odds of FCR > 0.1 mg/L after adjustment (aOR = 0.47, 95% CI: 0.31–0.72; mOR = 0.56, 95% CI: 0.34–0.92, p < 0.05); WSP was not significantly associated with under-5 diarrhea in multivariable models in 2016 (aOR = 1.03, 95% CI: 0.75–1.40) or 2017 (aOR = 0.82, 95% CI: 0.58–1.17).

mechanism_certainty.comment: Cross-sectional survey design is capped at 2 under CODEBOOK.md §9; coded as 1 (documented association) because the study establishes statistical and descriptive associations between community WSP programming, household water expenditure burden, piped vs. private vendor supply, and WASH/water-quality outcomes, while market regulation and targeted subsidy mechanisms are inferred/recommended rather than directly observed administratively.

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines household financial burden of purchasing water from private vendors (IncomeSpent ~20.5%–21.9% of income; hygiene item unaffordability), community-based WSP mobilization and volunteer monitoring networks (participation), and fragmented WASH governance across conflict-affected utilities, unregulated private water tankers, and Whole of Syria cross-border humanitarian hub coordination under UNSCR 2165 (institutional_fragmentation, political_coordination). Note: mention of international economic sanctions in Background (p. 2) is geopolitical context rather than utility enforcement sanctions.

sample_size.comment: Households without children under 5 years of age were excluded prior to the main descriptive and regression analyses, yielding analytic samples of 1,281 households in 2016 and 1,360 households in 2017 from 1,825 and 1,921 complete household responses, respectively.
sample_size.value: 3,746 complete household survey responses across 17 sub-districts (64 communities: 50 in Dar'a, 14 in Quneitra) over two rounds (1,825 households in 2016; 1,921 households in 2017); analytic sample of 2,641 households with children < 5 years old (1,281 households in 2016 [971 Dar'a, 310 Quneitra]; 1,360 households in 2017 [1,112 Dar'a, 248 Quneitra]), with household drinking water FCR tested in 1,207 households (2016) and 1,344 households (2017)

study_design.comment: Secondary analysis of two rounds of stratified/systematic cross-sectional household survey and water-quality testing data collected by the Whole of Syria WASH Cluster (Amman hub), analyzed via two-sample t-tests and separate 2016 and 2017 univariate, forward-stepwise multivariable, and sub-district mixed-effect logistic regressions.
study_design.value: Repeated cross-sectional household surveys (June/July 2016 and February 2017) with household drinking water quality testing (FCR and pH) and univariate, forward-stepwise multivariable, and mixed-effects logistic regression analysis

In 2016 and 2017, 1281 and 1360 surveys were conducted.

quality of water delivered by unregulated vendors remains
